title: How our In-House Legal Team Uses Harvey to Work Smarter
author: John LaBarre

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: LaBarre accepts that access alone is insufficient and materially extends the proposition with a coordinated implementation model: identify workflows, mandate defined uses and align the department around repeatable practices. His verified DORA workflow also illustrates how human checking and reusable work product can turn AI use into operational value, though the evidence remains vendor-reported and largely internal or customer-estimated.
qs: The most common advice I give customers when they ask about how to roll out AI tools is that **organizations need to do more than just provide the tools**.

If you leave these choices to chance, your team will still see some benefit and efficiencies from using tools like Harvey, but it’s really only when you get your entire department moving in a consistent direction that you begin to see material and measurable returns on your investment.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that Harvey’s value depends on coordinated workflow adoption rather than tool acquisition alone, while framing current use as lawyer augmentation and reporting customer-estimated in-house savings. It does not resolve the cluster’s broader questions about vendor durability or structural disruption.
qs: The most common advice I give customers when they ask about how to roll out AI tools is that **organizations need to do more than just provide the tools**.
And remember, tools like Harvey are not meant to replace lawyers; rather they are meant to enhance them.

st.t: Shared infrastructure: Harvey proposes continuous client collaboration
st.an: LaBarre supports Harvey’s proposed direction by describing reusable, playbook-based workflows that handle familiar work while lawyers focus on novel issues, and by explicitly anticipating collaboration with outside counsel. His evidence primarily concerns Harvey’s internal legal team and future product plans, however, so it does not independently demonstrate continuous cross-organisation collaboration or its outcomes.
qs: And since more than 95% of redlines are things we’ve seen before, Harvey enables our team to quickly and efficiently resolve or revise customer redlines based on our playbooks.
Spoiler alert: If you’ve been looking to start using Harvey to collaborate with folks outside your organization (like your outside counsel), things are about to get even more interesting.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s application-layer and implementation claims through embedded legal workflows, reported operational savings, coordinated adoption and lawyer augmentation. Its evidence is primarily Harvey’s own experience, customer estimates and a company benchmark, and it does not establish—or directly argue for—durable competitive defensibility.
qs: ### Workflow Builder: Speeding up Vendor Reviews  Early this year we introduced [Workflow Builder](/blog/introducing-workflow-builder), which allows users to create their own agentic processes that leverage the power of Harvey’s AI.

If you leave these choices to chance, your team will still see some benefit and efficiencies from using tools like Harvey, but it’s really only when you get your entire department moving in a consistent direction that you begin to see material and measurable returns on your investment.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: Harvey is deployed selectively as a copilot for recurring contracting, document-analysis and compliance tasks, while lawyers verify and refine outputs and retain novel judgment. Its workflow examples, reported time savings and recommendation for coordinated department-wide implementation also align with the cluster’s emphasis on verification and operating-model redesign, though its evidence is largely internal, customer-reported or based on Harvey’s own benchmark.
qs: And remember, tools like Harvey are not meant to replace lawyers; rather they are meant to enhance them.
The most common advice I give customers when they ask about how to roll out AI tools is that **organizations need to do more than just provide the tools**.

kp.k: Harvey reports expanding adoption alongside company growth
kp.d: LaBarre situates the internal legal team's changing practices within Harvey's growth since the previous year's post: approximately 200 employees became nearly 500, customers exceeded 700, and usage reached over 50% of the AmLaw 100. These are company-reported adoption figures, rather than measurements of legal productivity.
qs: Since last year, our company has grown from about 200 people to nearly 500.
We now work with more than 700 customers, Harvey is used by over 50% of the AmLaw 100, and we’re seeing strong adoption across EMEA and Australia.

kp.k: Custom workflows automate repetitive vendor-review tasks
kp.d: The author describes Workflow Builder as enabling user-created agentic processes composed of linked user-input, AI-action, logic and output blocks. Customers reportedly built over 15K workflows, while Harvey's team built dozens. Its Privacy team supplies vendor details and documentation to generate summaries and requirements-to-commitments comparisons covering privacy and security obligations, helping identify gaps during onboarding.
qs: Each workflow consists of linked steps and each step consists of one of four types of blocks: user input, AI action, logic, or output.

To date, our customers have built over 15K custom workflows and our own team has built out dozens of [workflows](/blog/getting-started-with-workflow-builder-5-workflows-we-recommend) to help automate certain repetitive tasks.

Harvey returns a concise summary of the key terms and a side‑by‑side table mapping our requirements to the vendor’s commitments — covering incident notification timelines, international data transfers, data use permissions, data in scope, data retention, and other core privacy and security obligations.

kp.k: Vendor-review savings retain verification and human decision-making
kp.d: LaBarre reports that the Privacy workflow took about an hour to create and refine, saves at least 4–6 hours weekly, and is estimated to save at least 2–3 hours per relevant procurement engagement. He states that findings are validated against source documents, final decisions remain human-led, and existing security and privacy controls apply. These are internal reported savings and controls.
qs: Most notably, every finding is validated against the source documents, and final decisions remain human‑led.
The workflow operates within our existing security and privacy controls, accelerating review without expanding risk.
It took Cory about an hour to create and finetune this workflow, saving his team at least 4-6 hours every week**.
We estimate that this workflow saves us an average of **at least 2-3 hours of work for each such engagement**.

kp.k: Playbook-based redlining shifts lawyers toward unfamiliar issues
kp.d: Harvey's Word integration generates responsive redlines and explanatory comments using the Commercial Legal team's playbook of acceptable fallbacks and negotiating positions. LaBarre says lawyers retain control over edits and that more than 95% of incoming redlines concern previously encountered issues, allowing commercial lawyers to concentrate on issues of first impression.
qs: When a customer sends us redlines, we can use Harvey right from within Word and generate responsive redlines automatically based on our playbook.
Harvey will even draft comment bubbles to help explain our position.
By using our own playbooks, Harvey is grounded in our risk tolerances, our acceptable language, and our logic.

And since more than 95% of redlines are things we’ve seen before, Harvey enables our team to quickly and efficiently resolve or revise customer redlines based on our playbooks. This frees our commercial lawyers to focus on the redlines of first impression.

kp.k: AI becomes embedded in nearly every commercial matter
kp.d: The author contrasts earlier use several times daily with the latest Word add-in's use on nearly every commercial matter. Many attorneys reportedly now work alongside Harvey for hours daily. He claims a substantial productivity impact, without quantifying that impact for commercial matters.
qs: In the past, I could confidently say that Harvey lawyers used Harvey regularly (at least several times a day).

Now, with the latest version of the Harvey for Word Add-In, our Commercial Legal team uses Harvey on nearly every single commercial matter that we work on, and many of our attorneys **spend hours every day working side-by-side with Harvey**.

kp.k: Document extraction produces reusable regulatory compliance materials
kp.d: LaBarre reports that Vault's document limit increased from 10,000 to 100,000. In an internal DORA example, the Head of EMEA Legal used a small collection of standard contracts to identify provisions addressing third-party ICT provider requirements, verified references against source language, and created reusable customer-facing collateral. The reported completion time fell from usually over five hours to just under two hours; the example does not describe testing at the maximum document capacity.
qs: Recently, we changed the document limit from 10,000 documents to 100,000 documents, making Vault even more useful for larger organizations.
She verified the results by using the source notes to help her quickly identify the specific language Harvey was referencing.
Now, we have a great piece of collateral that shows how each of the DORA-required third-party ICT service provider provisions are memorialized in our commercial paper.

Using Harvey, **a project that usually takes over five hours took just under two hours to complete** and we now have a defined piece of collateral that we can use to support this conversation whenever it comes up in the future.

kp.k: Prompt assistance supports learning and source-grounded responses
kp.d: LaBarre says the Improve button reformulates prompts and has improved his own prompting skills. The nudge feature recommends relevant knowledge sources, including Web Search and the paid LexisNexis integration, which permits users to open cited cases in full text. He presents these features as improving initial responses and grounding them in authoritative sources, without reporting measured accuracy results.
qs: Not only does using the Improve button yield better results the first time around, it has also helped me become a better prompter in the first instance.
While the LexisNexis integration is not a free option for customers (it’s a paid add-on), it is a great companion resource for certain kinds of work.

Here, I’ve selected the LexisNexis knowledge source and Harvey has come back with some relevant cases (and, if I click on the sources, I’m deeplinked right into LexisNexis to review the full text of the cited cases).

kp.k: Customer time-saving claims span multiple in-house legal functions
kp.d: The blog relays customer-reported benefits: Deutsche Telekom estimates five hours reclaimed per attorney user weekly across deployment in German Legal, Compliance and Data Protection; Adecco lawyers report up to eight hours saved weekly on routine work; Repsol reports 96% adoption in a 200-person Legal team and estimates four to six hours saved per lawyer weekly, compared with about three during its early pilot. These are customer claims carried by Harvey, not a common comparative study.
qs: reclaim an estimated five hours of attorney time per user per week
Their use cases include litigation support, public tenders, and regulatory compliance.
saving up to eight hours per week

They have **96% Harvey adoption** across their Legal department, and they estimate that they **save four to six hours per lawyer per week** (up from about three hours saved during their early pilot with Harvey).

kp.k: Syngenta estimates financial savings from its legal deployment
kp.d: The author reports Syngenta's estimate that a 40-seat deployment saved $320K in six months. The document does not explain the calculation or distinguish cash savings from the monetary value of time saved.
qs: They estimate that their 40-seat deployment of Harvey has **saved them $320K in just six months**.

kp.k: Material returns require directed departmental adoption
kp.d: LaBarre recommends identifying use cases, mandating tool use and setting explicit expectations for how staff use AI, rather than merely providing access. He argues that discretionary use still delivers some efficiencies, but consistent department-wide implementation is necessary for material, measurable returns.
qs: They need to identify use cases, mandate that these tools be used, and set expectations around how and on what folks are expected to be using AI.

If you leave these choices to chance, your team will still see some benefit and efficiencies from using tools like Harvey, but it’s really only when you get your entire department moving in a consistent direction that you begin to see material and measurable returns on your investment.

kp.k: Author advocates augmentation, citing a contract-review benchmark
kp.d: LaBarre frames Harvey as enhancing rather than replacing lawyers. He cites linked benchmark results claiming that lawyers working with Harvey outperform by 5% when reviewing contracts and producing structured analytical data, compared with lawyers alone or reliance entirely on LLMs. The supplied document gives no sample size, performance metric or methodological details.
qs: And remember, tools like Harvey are not meant to replace lawyers; rather they are meant to enhance them.

Check out our [recent benchmark results](/blog/contract-intelligence-benchmark) showing that **lawyers working in combination with Harvey** **outperform by 5%** on reviewing contracts and producing structured, analytical data (compared to performing the task by themselves or entirely relying on LLMs for such work).

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: John LaBarre presents Harvey as augmenting in-house legal teams through faster reviews, drafting, extraction and research, rather than replacing lawyers.
pts.d: LaBarre claims that a custom vendor-review workflow saves Harvey's Privacy team at least 4–6 hours weekly and an estimated 2–3 hours per relevant procurement engagement, while preserving human decisions and existing controls. He says playbook-based redlining in Word accelerates familiar negotiations and frees commercial lawyers to address novel issues; more than 95% of redlines are described as previously encountered. Vault is claimed to accelerate document extraction and compliance mapping: a DORA contract-mapping project reportedly fell from over five hours to under two hours and produced reusable customer collateral. He also claims the Improve button produces better initial responses and improves users' prompting, while source-selection nudges help ground answers in authoritative material. LaBarre relays customer-reported gains: Deutsche Telekom estimates five attorney hours recovered per user weekly; Adecco lawyers report up to eight hours weekly and an example of improved litigation preparedness; Repsol estimates four to six hours per lawyer weekly; Syngenta estimates $320,000 saved over six months. He argues that coordinated, mandated adoption is needed for material, measurable returns and cites a benchmark claim that lawyers using Harvey outperform lawyers alone or exclusive reliance on LLMs by 5% on contract review and structured analysis. Looking toward 2026, he predicts continued productivity improvements and hints at forthcoming collaboration with external parties such as outside counsel.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of internal usage experience and time estimates, customer reports, adoption figures and a linked benchmark; future claims rest on roadmap expectations.
pts.d: This is LaBarre's December 2, 2025 company-blog account. Internal examples identify Cory's vendor-review workflow and Sally's DORA mapping exercise, including source verification and preparation of reusable collateral. The text does not supply timing protocols, sample sizes or controlled comparisons for those productivity estimates. The Word and prompting claims rely on reported experience rather than quantified performance tests. Customer savings are explicitly estimates or lawyer reports, linked to customer material; Repsol's 96% adoption across a 200-person legal team and Syngenta's 40-seat deployment provide deployment context, not independent measures of output quality. LaBarre links recent contract-intelligence benchmark results for the 5% augmentation claim, but the supplied text does not specify the metric, sample, methodology or whether 5% denotes a relative improvement or percentage-point difference. Other scale indicators include over 15,000 customer-created workflows, dozens of internal workflows, an increased Vault document limit and over 120 features introduced during 2025. These support his account of product development and use, rather than directly establishing savings. The 2026 collaboration suggestion is a forward-looking product teaser without outcome evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims describe current or recent 2025 use, conditional on configured workflows, organizational playbooks, human verification and directed adoption; further gains are predicted for 2026.
pts.d: Workflow Builder was introduced early in 2025 and the latest Word add-in a few months before publication. Vendor-review savings follow roughly an hour of workflow creation and refinement and apply to procurement involving personal information, with relevant documentation supplied. Findings are checked against sources and final decisions remain human-led. Redlining gains depend on Harvey applying the team's risk tolerances, fallback language and reasoning through its playbook, with lawyers retaining control over edits; the account concerns negotiations generally conducted on Harvey's own contract forms. The DORA example includes human source verification and formatting refinement, and its reusable collateral is expected to help on subsequent customer inquiries. Source nudges depend on suitable knowledge-source access; LexisNexis is a paid add-on. Customer figures cover weekly time savings, a six-month Syngenta deployment and a Repsol comparison with an earlier pilot. LaBarre conditions substantial returns on identifying use cases, requiring use and setting shared expectations, while acknowledging some benefits from less coordinated adoption. His outlook for 2026 offers no precise release date or quantified forecast for external collaboration.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects primarily concern corporate in-house legal, privacy and compliance teams, their business counterparts and enterprise customers; outside counsel appear as prospective collaborators.
pts.d: Harvey's Privacy team and Senior Privacy and AI Program Manager gain faster identification of vendor security and privacy gaps, supporting procurement. Commercial lawyers gain drafting assistance on recurring contract objections and more time for novel negotiation issues. The Head of EMEA Legal uses verified contract mapping to support EU financial-sector customers' DORA inquiries. Large organizations are presented as beneficiaries of Vault's increase from 10,000 to 100,000 documents. Customer examples cover Deutsche Telekom's German Legal, Compliance and Data Protection departments, Adecco lawyers, Repsol's 200-person Legal team and Syngenta's global Legal team. Department leaders are tasked with organizing adoption and expectations. The account frames these changes as greater capacity, efficiency and supported professional judgment, not reductions in legal staffing. Although adoption by over half of the AmLaw 100 is mentioned as company context, the article does not establish corresponding law-firm staffing, pricing or market-structure effects. It makes no access-to-justice claim.
